source: Wang & Sun (2025) Unable to Forget: Proactive Interference Reveals Working Memory Limits in LLMs Beyond Context Length (PI-LLM)
finding: LLM version of proactive interference. A stream of key-value updates is shown, then only the final value of each key is asked. Accuracy falls roughly log-linearly as the number of overwritten values grows. Errors are mostly retrieval of old, overwritten values.
numbers: Exp 1: 46 keys, 3 to 400 updates per key (log-spaced). A group of mid-size models drops to 0% at 400 updates; larger models stay relatively high (no figure given in text). Models from Qwen3-0.6B to DeepSeek-V3 (637B). Trial count not stated.
limits: Synthetic task. Slope and IES values only in figures. Exact model list truncated in the page text I read (last 5,860 characters unread).
agent_relevance: Direct measurement that many similar, superseded entries in context hurt retrieval of the current one. Supports capping similar entries per class and removing superseded ones.

source: Wang & Sun (2025) PI-LLM: fixed-length controls and value length
finding: Interference hurts even when total input length is held fixed. Tracking more keys among the same updates lowers accuracy. Longer values make it worse.
numbers: Exp 2B: U=46 updated keys fixed, tracked keys T=1 to 46, same input length: llama4-maverick near 100% at 2 tracked keys, below 5% at 46. Exp 3: 20 updates, value length up to 40 words: under 40% for every model at 10 words, under 5% at 40 words.
limits: Single synthetic paradigm; sequential order shows step-like collapse at a model-specific threshold rather than gradual decay.
agent_relevance: Interference load, not token count, is the driver. Context length budgets alone do not protect the agent; the count of competing similar items does.

source: Wang & Sun (2025) PI-LLM: model size vs context window, reasoning, mitigations
finding: Parameter size predicts interference endurance; context window length does not. Chain-of-thought does not help. Prompt-only forget instructions help little. A mock Q&A reset inserted before the query helps most.
numbers: N=30 open models regression: size class t=3.03, p=0.005; context length t=-0.144, p=0.886; R2=0.261. Within 128k-131k models Spearman rho2=0.673, p=0.0016. Per-key forget prompt change under 10 points at 100 updates. Mock QA reset: Gemini Flash 2.0 at 150 updates matched its baseline at 30-45 updates. CoT worse or equal in 3 of 4 pairs; DeepSeek-R1 below V3 beyond 12 updates.
quote: Model size, not context window length, is the primary factor
limits: Regression is observational across heterogeneous models (R2 only 0.26). MoE models below dense at similar total size.
agent_relevance: Telling the model to ignore old items is weak. A structural reset or removal done in code beats an instruction. Do not rely on extra reasoning to fix interference.

source: Chattaraj & Raj (2026) LLMs Remember First, Forget Last: Dual-Process Interference in LLMs
finding: AB-AC paired-associate logic moved into context updates. First-value queries (retroactive style) and latest-value queries (proactive style) use identical input. Across 39 LLMs the latest-value query collapses far more than the first-value query.
numbers: 39 models with full data (54 tested), 1B to 2.5T params. N=3,10,50,100,200,300 assignments per category; 46 categories. RI accuracy 93.9% (N=3), 96.0% (N=50), 72.9% (N=100), 45.5% (N=200), 24.6% (N=300). PI accuracy from about 94% to about 3%. PIES lower than RIES for all 39, mean gap 69.5 points, Cohen d=1.73. Temperature 0, up to 50 sessions per standard model.
limits: One paradigm, transformers only, English, temp 0. Mechanism claims (superposition, attention sinks) are post hoc and untested. Proprietary parameter counts are estimates.
agent_relevance: Old-first items and newest items fail differently. The agent cannot assume that the most recent entry wins; code must resolve which entry is current.

source: Chattaraj & Raj (2026) Dual-process interference: scale, reasoning models and error types
finding: Size predicts retroactive-type resistance but not proactive-type. RI and PI resistance are uncorrelated across models. Most errors are same-key intrusions (right category, wrong position), not invented values. Reasoning models do better on RI but not PI.
numbers: Parameter count explains 49% of RIES variance (R2=0.49) but 6% of PIES (R2=0.06, ns). RI vs PI endurance r=0.21 (95% CI -0.11 to 0.49). Reasoning models mean RIES 178.0 vs 150.3 (d=1.76); o1 RIES 186.4 but PIES 22.0. PI errors: 42.5% retrieval failure, 56.1% same-key intrusion, 0.2% hallucination, 8.6% refusals. At N=3 PI intrusions come from early positions (0.12), 14% return the first value. PI at N>=200 bimodal: above 85% or below 5% per session.
limits: n=39 gives low power for moderate correlations. Mitigations (recency re-weighting, ordering) proposed but not tested.
agent_relevance: Interference errors are confusions with real earlier values. A code check against a keyed current-value table catches them; a model self-check would not.

source: Shahrabi-Farahani & Rahmati (2026) Compress and Forget: bitsandbytes Quantization Amplifies Proactive Interference in LLMs
finding: 4-bit quantization makes PI worse. 8-bit hurts less. The effect traces to the quantized transformer backbone, appears with semantically similar distractors, and reverses with a numeric control.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, Phi-3.5-mini. Qwen accuracy at high interference 81.0% (FP16) to 68.3% (INT4); McNemar p<=2.6e-6. Same-key intrusions 21.5% to 24.6% (p=4.8e-7). INT8 penalty in 2 of 3 models.
limits: Abstract page only was read (not the full text). Three small models, one retrieval task.
agent_relevance: If the agent ever runs on a quantized local model, interference limits tighten. Set any per-class cap with margin.

source: SleepGate (2026) Learning to Forget: Sleep-Inspired Memory Consolidation for Resolving PI in LLMs
finding: A learned gate tags superseded KV-cache entries as stale (by similarity to a newer entry), biases attention away from them and merges clusters. On a PI-LLM-style task it beats cache-eviction baselines by a wide margin, but only at shallow depth.
numbers: Tiny 4-layer transformer trained from scratch (793k params), 100 entities, 200 episodes per depth. SleepGate accuracy: 99.0% (n=2), 99.5% (n=5), 97.0% (n=10), 73.5% (n=15), 30.5% (n=20), 16.5% (n=30; 62% stale retrieval). All baselines (full KV cache, sliding window, H2O, StreamingLLM, decay-only) under 18% at every depth; full cache 2.5% at n=30.
limits: Synthetic, from-scratch, no pretrained models. Abstract claims O(log n) horizon but the theorem gives a bound constant in n. Hard eviction untested.
agent_relevance: Flagging an entry as superseded by a newer similar one is the working move. This matches keep-the-latest done in code.

source: Sculptor (2025) Empowering LLMs with Cognitive Agency via Active Context Management
finding: Giving a model tools to fragment, fold and search its context removes obsolete items and improves PI-LLM accuracy; trained with RL it nearly solves it. Untrained models barely use the fold tool unless told to.
numbers: PI-LLM, 2 to 256 updates over 46 keys. Prompt-guided: Claude-4-Sonnet 84.04 to 89.94 (+5.90), GPT-4.1 73.29 to 79.87 (+6.58), DeepSeek-V3 57.39 to 57.27. Trained 13B: baseline 22.5, +RAG 17.9, +MemAgent 41.5, Sculptor-M3 71.8, Sculptor-M3-RL 99.4. Context cut from 72.4K to 8.0K tokens (89%). 43 of 46 keys (93.5%) got more attention when folded.
limits: In-progress work. Unguided Claude-4-Sonnet used search for 90.7% of tool calls and used its 20-call budget without filtering. Gains modest on LongBenchV2 (+1.5), FRAMES (-0.6).
agent_relevance: Evidence that removing stale items from context, not asking the model to ignore them, fixes PI. Code can decide what to drop.

source: Hong, Troynikov & Huber (2025) Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance (Chroma)
finding: In needle-in-haystack tasks, adding distractors that resemble the needle lowers accuracy, and four distractors are worse than one. Hallucinated answers often come from the distractors. Lower needle-question similarity degrades faster with length.
numbers: 18 LLMs, 8 input lengths, 11 needle positions. Conditions: 0, 1, 4 distractors. Needle-question cosine similarity (mean of 5 embedders, SD<0.1): PG essays 0.445-0.775, arXiv 0.521-0.829. Shuffled haystacks beat structured ones in all 18. 69 of 194,480 calls refused.
limits: No exact accuracy numbers in text (charts only). Only two haystack topics. Authors note length is confounded with difficulty; LLM judges used.
agent_relevance: Similar-but-wrong entries act like interference. Supports varying category and keeping near-duplicates out of one retrieval set.

source: Hong et al. (2025) Context Rot: LongMemEval focused vs full prompts
finding: On LongMemEval, models do better with a focused prompt of about 300 tokens than with the full ~113k-token history, though the answer is in both.
numbers: 306 prompts; ~113k tokens full vs ~300 focused; all models significantly higher on focused. Claude gap largest, mostly from abstentions.
limits: Does not isolate interference from length and general distraction.
agent_relevance: Retrieval into a small clean working set beats dumping full memory in. Selection by code before the model sees entries.

source: Mittal (2026) Did You Forget What I Asked? Prospective Memory Failures in LLMs
finding: Instruction compliance drops when the model must also do a demanding task, and extra constraints hurt task accuracy in turn. A salient reminder format recovers most of it.
numbers: 3 model families, over 8,000 prompts. Compliance drops 2-21% under load; terminal constraints up to 50%. Salient format restores 90-100% in many settings. One model GSM8K 93% to 27% with formatting constraints added. Deterministic checkers.
limits: Abstract page only. This is task-load interference, not list-based PI/RI; the link is by analogy.
agent_relevance: Competing demands interfere both ways. Keep constraints few and restate them near the output slot.

source: Kerestecioglu et al. (2026) Human-Inspired Memory Architecture for LLM Agents
finding: Agent memory design with an interference score. Similar stored memories are scored by pairwise similarity and weighted retroactive 0.6, proactive 0.4. High-interference, low-value memories are forgotten. The 0.6/0.4 weights are asserted from the human literature, not measured.
numbers: Interference threshold set at P90 of within-session similarity (0.542, text-embedding-3-large). Near-dedup threshold at P99 (0.559). VSCode issues: 13,127 issues, 120,000 events; consolidation plus forgetting gives 97.2% retention precision with 58% store reduction vs 75.4% keep-everything (+21.8 points). Store self-regulates at 300-500 events.
limits: VSCode metric is retention precision, not QA. The paper credits dedup consolidation for most of the gain; no ablation of the interference term alone was seen. Weights are not validated.
agent_relevance: Concrete recipe close to our memory rule: similarity threshold at a percentile, keep one per cluster. Treat the 0.6/0.4 weights as a placeholder.

source: Kerestecioglu et al. (2026) Human-Inspired Memory Architecture: LongMemEval M-tier
finding: On long histories the forgetting pipeline does not beat plain retrieval over raw turns. Aggressive token budgets lose accuracy.
numbers: LongMemEval M-tier, 475 sessions, GPT-4o. Raw RAG k=10: 71.2% overall [67.2, 75.0]. Dedup-adaptive at 200K tokens: 70.1% [66.0, 74.2]; lower budgets fell to about 65.6%, 49.2%, 38.8% (115K, 50K, 25K by my reading of a garbled table). Multi-session +1.2, temporal +3.0 vs raw RAG at 200K.
limits: Table text was garbled by PDF extraction; row-to-value mapping for the lower budgets is my best reading. Single backbone.
agent_relevance: Forgetting by code did not help here. Pruning similar entries can cost recall when the history is genuinely diverse.

source: Diagnosing retrieval vs utilization bottlenecks in LLM agent memory (2026), arXiv:2603.02473
finding: On LoCoMo, retrieval method matters more than how memory is written. Failures are mostly retrieval failures, not the model failing to use retrieved memory. No interference analysis.
numbers: LoCoMo, 10 conversations, 1,540 questions, GPT-5-mini. Accuracy: cosine 73.4, BM25 57.1, hybrid+rerank 77.2. Retrieval failure 11.4% to 46.3% of questions; utilization failure 3.9-8.1%. Precision@5 vs accuracy r=0.98. Raw chunking 77.9 (cosine) beat extracted facts 72.2.
limits: Does not test interference. One model, one benchmark, k=5. Authors not read.
agent_relevance: Lossy rewriting at write time did not beat raw storage with good retrieval. Do not assume more memory processing reduces interference.

source: Peterson & Peterson (1959) Short-term retention of individual verbal items. J Exp Psychol 58:193-198
finding: The Brown-Peterson paradigm. One consonant trigram, then counting backward by 3 or 4, then recall. Recall falls within seconds. The authors fitted a stimulus-fluctuation (Estes) model, not interference.
numbers: Exp I: 24 students, 48 trigrams, 8 trials at each of 3,6,9,12,15,18 s, counting to a 2 per second metronome. All differences among the 3-,6-,9-,12-,18-s conditions significant at .05; 3 vs 18 s at .01. Exp II: 48 students; the vocal group recall at 3/9/18 s rose with controlled repetition: 3 s repetition about .80/.48/.34, 1 s about .68/.34/.21, 0 s about .60/.25/.14 (row labels garbled in extraction, values as read).
limits: Table layout garbled by extraction; do not quote single cells. Items chosen as dissimilar to limit interference.
agent_relevance: Original data for fast forgetting without list interference. The authors argued stimulus fluctuation first; later work reinterpreted it as PI.

source: Peterson & Peterson (1959): their own test for proactive interference in Exp I
finding: The authors checked for proactive interference by splitting trials into four blocks and found none. Short intervals even improved with practice. Keppel and Underwood (1962) later argued PI is the cause of the forgetting.
numbers: Proportion correct over successive blocks of 12 presentations, 3 and 6 s combined: .57, .66, .70, .74 (first vs last block, sign test p=.02, an improvement). 15 and 18 s: .08, .15, .09, .12 (gain not significant).
quote: There is no evidence for proactive interference.
limits: Blocks mix intervals, so few trials per interval to see buildup. Items were deliberately dissimilar. This is a failure to find PI that later work overturned.
agent_relevance: PI needs similar prior items and enough of them. With dissimilar materials it can be absent.

source: Turvey, Mosher & Katz (1971) Subsequent recognition of items subjected to PI in STM. Psychon Sci 25:364-366
finding: Five successive 18-s Brown-Peterson tests with country-name triads show PI buildup. A later recognition test shows non-recalled items were still stored. Forgetting in the series looks like retrieval and discrimination failure, plus failure of later items to enter or stay in storage.
numbers: N=90 students, 5 tests, 15 country names plus 30 new in recognition; false positive rate .09. Recognition of recalled items about .92 to .98; non-recalled items about .58 to .76 (mean .68).
limits: Table 1 partly garbled in extraction; values read as ranges. Recall means appear only in a figure.
agent_relevance: Items that cannot be recalled are often still stored. Interference is access failure, so better cues and fewer competitors help more than re-storing.

source: Underwood (1957) Interference and forgetting. Psychol Rev 64:49-60 (as summarized by Wixted 2004)
finding: Underwood asked why one-day forgetting of a list learned to one perfect recall differed so much between studies. The number of prior lists learned in the lab explained nearly all the spread. He concluded proactive interference is the main cause of laboratory forgetting and retroactive interference is probably minor.
numbers: One-day forgetting ranged from about 20% to nearly 80% across studies. Few prior lists meant much less forgetting.
quote: nearly all of the variability across studies could be explained by the number of prior lists
limits: Secondhand: read in Wixted's review, not in Underwood's own paper. Wixted notes Underwood included only studies where prior learning was massed.
agent_relevance: Forgetting depends on how much similar material came before. Fewer prior similar entries means better recall of the new one.

source: Underwood (1957) abstract figures
finding: The abstract is reported to say the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve is mainly due to interference from earlier laboratory material, and that forgetting falls from about 75% to about 25% over 24 h when this interference is removed.
numbers: 75% to 25% forgetting over 24 hours (quoted by a search-engine summary of the abstract).
limits: Not opened: scilit returned 403; the figure comes from a search summary. Differs in form from Wixted's 20% to 80% across studies.
agent_relevance: Same as above; verify before quoting.

source: Wixted (2004) The psychology and neuroscience of forgetting: limits of the PI account of everyday forgetting
finding: Underwood's later work showed PI appears when prior learning is massed but not when spread over days. Underwood and Postman (1960) found equal one-week forgetting for words and meaningless trigrams, against the unlearning prediction. Slamecka (1966) found no unlearning of old associations.
numbers: Underwood & Ekstrand (1966, 1967): PI shown with massed prior trials; none when spread over four days. Underwood & Postman (1960): forgetting rates the same for 3-letter words and 3-letter trigrams over one week.
limits: Wixted is a critic of the PI-centred story and his summary is selective. Primary papers not opened.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: PI in the lab is strongest with massed, similar prior material. In an agent, spaced and varied entries are the low-risk case.

source: Wixted (2004): sleep, Jenkins & Dallenbach (1924) and Ekstrand (1967)
finding: Jenkins & Dallenbach found more recall after sleep than after waking, taken as less retroactive interference. Underwood could not explain this with PI and guessed PI is off during sleep. Ekstrand (1967) tested it: sleep improved memory for both the A-B and A-C lists, so PI mechanisms are not off.
numbers: Ekstrand (1967): A-B then A-C lists learned late at night with 8 h sleep vs in the morning with 8 h awake; both lists better after sleep. Other secondary sources give the 1924 design as 2 subjects, 10-syllable lists, 1, 2, 4, 8 h (not opened).
limits: The 1924 figures were not obtained from a primary source. Wixted reads sleep as consolidation, a competing account to interference.
agent_relevance: Competing explanation: some 'interference' may be un-consolidated memory disrupted by new activity. Agent writes are immediate, so this has no clear analogue.

source: Wixted (2004): Muller & Pilzecker (1900) and the temporal gradient of retroactive interference
finding: Muller & Pilzecker found a second list learned soon after the first impaired it, but not when learned later. They said traces need time to consolidate. Skaggs (1925) found RI from unrelated mental work such as algebra, and more RI with greater similarity.
numbers: List A (six syllable pairs), list X after 17 s or 6 min: A impaired on a cued recall 1.5 h later only in the 17 s case. Skaggs (1925): RI for chess positions, words, nonsense syllables, syllable pairs, even with dissimilar interpolated work.
limits: Secondhand via Wixted and Lechner et al. (1999); no English translation of the monograph. Not all of Skaggs's subjects showed the effect.
agent_relevance: Even unrelated activity can interfere; similarity makes it worse but is not required.

source: Wixted (2004): is the RI time gradient real? Archer & Underwood (1951), Newton & Wickens (1956), Postman & Alper (1946)
finding: The expected inverted-U of retroactive interference over time was weak. Archer and Underwood found it only in the high A-C learning group. Newton and Wickens found no significant effect in the standard test, but Wixted's reanalysis found one. Their A-B, C-D studies showed interference rising with delay, which no consolidation or interference account predicts.
numbers: Archer & Underwood: 10 A-B pairs, 48 h retention, A-C learned at 0, 24 or 48 h, nine groups of 10; quadratic trend in the high-learning group F(1,74)=2.83, p<.10. Newton & Wickens: quadratic trend F(1,54)=5.91, p<.05, using an error term borrowed from other experiments. Postman & Alper: 16-day interval, nine placement points.
limits: Low power and a post hoc reanalysis by a consolidation advocate. Mixed replication record.
agent_relevance: Timing effects of interference are weak and fragile. Do not build an agent rule on the timing of similar writes.

source: Mensink & Raaijmakers (1988) A model for interference and forgetting. Psychol Rev 95:434-455
finding: A formal model: SAM (search of associative memory) plus a contextual-fluctuation process. Memory images store item, associative and context elements. Retrieval strength is the overlap of the cue with each image. Competing images share cues, so more or stronger competitors lower the chance of retrieving the target. It needs no unlearning.
numbers: Context elements flip between active and inactive; rates .0035 (active to inactive) and .0001 (inactive to active); conditioning rate .6; context scale .3; interitem strength b1=b2=.05; residual d=.01. One parameter set for all simulations. Recovery probability 1-exp[-S(I,C)-S(I,Si)]. Search stops after Lmax attempts.
limits: Fits are qualitative only. The authors note a predicted growth of PI with retention interval was not seen in Underwood (1949) data and attribute it to floor effects.
agent_relevance: The formal core: P(retrieve) falls with the number and strength of other items sharing the cue. A usable rule for memory design.

source: Mensink & Raaijmakers (1988): history of the theory (McGeoch, Melton & Irwin, Barnes & Underwood)
finding: McGeoch (1932): three factors, response competition, change of situation between learning and test, and wrong set. Melton & Irwin (1940) added unlearning. Barnes & Underwood (1959) used modified modified free recall (MMFR) to support unlearning. PI was then found on MMFR tests too, where competition should be gone, and spontaneous recovery proved shaky.
numbers: PI on MMFR: Birnbaum 1965, Houston 1967, Koppenaal 1963, Slamecka 1966. Koppenaal (1963): no spontaneous recovery on MMFR. Postman, Stark & Fraser (1968): recovery only in special conditions. Postman & Underwood (1973) replaced unlearning with response-set suppression.
limits: The model authors' own account of the history; not independent.
agent_relevance: Several explanations stay live: competition, context drift, suppression. Unlearning is largely rejected, so do not tie design to it.

source: Mensink & Raaijmakers (1988): predictions and fits
finding: The model reproduces RI and PI, spontaneous recovery, independence of List 1 and List 2 recall, Osgood's transfer surface, simple forgetting curves and the accuracy-latency link. It also fits Anderson's (1981) reaction-time data.
numbers: Fit to Anderson (1981): a=1.47, b=0.07, d=0.0, B=0.011, gamma=0.012, Lmax=4.90, v=0.61, w=0.65. Removing one auxiliary assumption raised the chi-square loss to 110.86.
limits: Qualitative match for most classic data; later critics of SAM not covered here.
agent_relevance: Supports interference as retrieval competition plus context mismatch. A context change (new category, new framing) should lower it.

source: Keppel & Underwood (1962) Proactive inhibition in short-term retention of single items. JVLVB 1:153-161
finding: On the first trial of a Brown-Peterson procedure there is little or no forgetting over 3 to 18 s. Forgetting builds up over the first few trials. Read as proactive inhibition from earlier items, not time-based decay.
numbers: Build-up over the first 4 or 5 items; intervals of 3 and 18 s (secondary description). No exact percentages obtained.
limits: Not opened. Only secondary descriptions and Turvey et al. (1971) citing it. Exact trial-by-trial numbers missing.
agent_relevance: Forgetting a fresh item depends on how many earlier similar items came before it. Backs capping per class.

source: Wickens release from proactive inhibition (category-shift paradigm), via a secondary page
finding: Subjects do several trials of short-term recall with words from one category. Recall falls over trials 1 to 3 from PI. On trial 4, if the category changes, recall jumps back. Release size depends on how different the new category is.
numbers: Trials 2 and 3 lower, trial 4 higher after the switch (profession and meat conditions described). A thesis summary says release is bigger fruit to professions than fruit to vegetables. No percentages obtained.
limits: Primary not opened. The page itself ties the experiment to a dichotic-listening paper, so attribution is shaky. Wickens, Born & Allen (1963) is the primary source; Wickens (1970, 1972) not read.
agent_relevance: Direct empirical basis for varying category. A class shift resets the build-up.

source: Greenberg & Underwood (1950) retention as a function of stage of practice (via Wikipedia)
finding: Lists learned in sequence by the same people were forgotten more the later they came, which is proactive interference.
numbers: Ten paired adjectives, criterion 8 correct. Recall after two days about 70% (first list), about 40% (list learned the next day), about 25% (third list).
limits: Not opened: figures come from a Wikipedia summary of the paper. Unverified.
agent_relevance: Large PI effects in massed lab conditions: the upper bound of the effect.

source: Briggs (1954) and Barnes & Underwood (1959) on unlearning and recovery (via Wikipedia and Mensink & Raaijmakers)
finding: Briggs found B responses spontaneously recover after 24 h and exceed C. Barnes and Underwood's MMFR task suggested unlearning of A-B as A-C was learned. Later work challenged both.
numbers: Briggs (1954): 12 paired associates to 100% criterion; after 24 h B recall exceeded C. Barnes & Underwood: A-C responses still outnumbered A-B after the delay (Wikipedia summary).
limits: Primaries not opened. Mensink & Raaijmakers (opened) say spontaneous recovery proved unreliable and PI was found on MMFR tests too.
agent_relevance: The unlearning story is weak; do not copy it into agent design.

source: Kliegl & Baeuml (2021) The mechanisms underlying interference and inhibition. Brain Sci 11:1246
finding: Current review. In paired-associate tasks, A-B then A-D lists give worse recall than A-B then C-D; response competition explains this. Competition rises with more study cycles of the interfering list, though not in all studies. When people notice the change and recall the earlier response during study (recursive reminding), interference can turn into facilitation. In multiple-list tasks PI comes from retrieval (bigger search set) and encoding (less attention to later lists).
numbers: Latencies rise with extra lists (Wixted & Rohrer 1993); Unsworth et al. 2013 found more intrusions. A warning before the last list improved recall (Weinstein et al. 2014). EEG: theta (5-8 Hz) and alpha (10-13 Hz) rise after prior lists, less so in high working-memory individuals (Kliegl et al. 2015). Materials: syllable-noun, noun-noun, odour-picture, picture-word, color-word pairs.
limits: A review: figures cited from other papers; some effects of study repetition conflict ('but see' refs). Mostly word materials.
agent_relevance: Two levers: noticing change at write time (link the new entry to the old one) and limiting the search set. Both map to memory design.

source: Baeuml & Kliegl (2013) The critical role of retrieval processes in release from PI. J Mem Lang 68:39-53
finding: Replicates Wixted & Rohrer (1993): prior lists lower recall and slow later responses. Three release methods (forget cue, testing the earlier list, context change) restore recall and speed. Release works by shrinking the search set.
numbers: Exp 1A (N=24 on totals, 21 on latency): no-PI vs remember cue difference 14.58%, t(23)=4.263, p<.001, d=1.342; forget vs remember 11.27%, t(23)=3.491, p=.002, d=1.069; no-PI vs forget n.s. (p=.173), near-complete release. Subsequent-response latency: remember 10.73 s, no-PI 9.29 s (diff 1.44 s, p=.049); forget about 9.18 s (1.55 s faster than remember, p=.035; 0.11 s from no-PI, ns). Intrusions 4.51% forget vs 2.26% remember (ns).
limits: Small samples. Subsequent-response latency, not first-response, drove the effect. Four experiments; only Exp 1A read in detail. Forget-condition latency is derived from the reported differences.
agent_relevance: A forget or reset signal restores performance by cutting competing items. Agent analogue: drop superseded notes from the working set, not just mark them.

source: Anderson & Neely (1996) Interference and inhibition in memory retrieval; Anderson (2003) Rethinking interference theory
finding: Anderson argues forgetting from interference is not only passive overwriting. Control processes suppress competing memories during retrieval (retrieval-induced forgetting). Kliegl & Baeuml (opened) contrast this with the blocking account.
numbers: No numbers obtained.
limits: Not opened: only abstracts and citations seen.
agent_relevance: Retrieving one item can lower later access to similar unpracticed items. Test before assuming it applies to an agent.
